item.title: Episode 6: Google DeepMind No Longer Has a CEO
item.itunes:author: Anmol
item.description:
On Wednesday 5 August, Sundar Pichai's blog post moved Demis Hassabis to Chair of GDM and Chief Scientist of Alphabet, made Koray Kavukcuoglu **SVP of Google DeepMind reporting to Pichai — not CEO, whatever several outlets wrote** — and confirmed Jeff Dean's departure after 27 years to launch Discovery Loop with Sanjay Ghemawat, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le. Google DeepMind now has no chief executive, and the semi-independent layer between DeepMind and Google is gone. Plus CoreBreak, the Black Hat research showing an agent runtime can be made to fire its own tools with no model turn at all, Alphabet's up-to-$25bn bond raise, Canva cutting its growth forecast on AI serving costs, Google Maps becoming a transacting agent, and an AI that designed 16 working bacteriophages.
## In this episode
- **CoreBreak** — Hedi Ingber and Aviyam Ivgi at Black Hat USA. Data *shaped like* a model-generated tool call reaches the dispatch path and the runtime executes it, with no model turn. **This is not prompt injection.** AWS, Google and Vercel all shipped fixes — **and the exposure is still not closed**: the open-source **Strands** library AgentCore is built on retains the vulnerable shortcut, a PR raising it was **closed unmerged on 19 June 2026**, and AWS issued documentation rather than a code patch on shared-responsibility grounds - **CoreBreak is NOT episode 5's Check Point research.** Different researchers, different bugs, same conference. Google **did** issue CVE-2026-18236 (CVSS 9.3) for the CoreBreak ADK flaw and **did not** issue one for Check Point's separate ADK finding, which got a partial fix. Caveat per The Hacker News: the public CVE record covers the continuation-forgery path only, and ADK 2.5.0 also fixed a second bypass with no CVE assigned - **Alphabet returns to the bond market** — up to **$25bn**, in as many as **10 parts**, maturities 2–40 years, ~$115bn peak demand. Context: Q2 capex of $44.9bn and negative free cash flow of about $5.9bn - **Canva cuts its growth forecast** — to around **20%, down from a 30% target**. That is a cut to the **growth rate, not to revenue**. Quarterly revenue reported at about **US$922m**. Perkins: the average cost of serving an AI task was too high. Recovery: **90% off the cost of one AI task**, a video model **17×** and an image model **30×** cheaper than **an unnamed frontier model** - **Google Maps becomes a transacting agent** — Ask Maps orders food (Square and Toast, US only), compares hotels, buys tickets. **Personal Intelligence**, which reads Gmail and Calendar, is **off by default**. Plus Gemini Spark driving your real desktop Chrome - **An AI designed 16 working viruses** — Stanford and the Arc Institute went from just over 300 generated bacteriophage designs to 16 that infected *E. coli* strain C, with Johns Hopkins' Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke asking for an ID check at the DNA synthesis provider that **no US law currently requires**. Context most coverage omitted: **Thursday is the peer-reviewed publication in *Science*; the work has been public as a preprint since September 2025.** The capability didn't appear this week — it finished review this week - **Follow-up with a clock:** CISA's 7 August federal deadline on **CVE-2026-9198** passed with **still no published exploitation detail and no threat-actor attribution**. What is new is the exploitation chain, described by security vendors rather than CISA. (Added to the KEV catalog **Tuesday 4 August**, per CISA's own alert page) - **Deep dive:** the restructure, Discovery Loop (**no disclosed raise or valuation — the round was still open**), Alphabet shares falling about 4% on Wednesday, the six-month coding gap Semafor's sources describe, and five named counter-arguments that do not agree with each other

item.title: Episode 5: The Agent Industry Has Been Guarding the Wrong Door
item.itunes:author: Anmol
item.description:
Check Point researchers spent about a year attacking the frameworks AI agents run on rather than the models, and disclosed 11 vulnerabilities at Black Hat USA — insecure deserialization, SSRF, path traversal, use-after-free, all bug classes the industry learned to fix twenty years ago. The same week, CISA added an unauthenticated RCE in Langflow OSS (IBM) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with a federal remediation deadline of Friday 7 August. Plus Meta's Muse Code and the tier where the discount is paid for in developer data, Cloudflare handing agents an identity and a wallet (handle reservation is all that's live), the White House framework that reportedly defines "covered frontier model" and still won't be published, and a containment failure that is *not* the story everyone is merging it with.
## In this episode
- **Meta ships Muse Code** and Muse Spark 1.2 — pricing per 1M tokens on both tiers, the contributor discount (21.25× on **output tokens**, 12.5× input, 75× cached input), the rate-limit gap nobody quotes, and what contributors actually hand over — most coverage says permission to train on your prompts and completions, with Engadget the outlier - **Meta loses on its own benchmarks** — its published comparison puts Muse Spark 1.2 behind Claude Opus 5, and its OpenAI comparator is GPT-5.6 Terra, not Sol - **Cloudflare Wallets and cloudflare.pay** — account wallets, virtual wallets, stablecoins over x402. What is actually live today is **handle reservation**. No fees disclosed. Plus Cloudflare OS open-sourced under Apache 2.0 - **The White House framework** mandated by EO 14409 was reviewed on 4 August and will not be published. **Axios reported** it defines a covered frontier model as closed-source and excludes open models — reporting about a secret document, not a published rule - **A second containment failure**, at evaluation firm Irregular: an OpenAI model exploited a real site after a misconfiguration left the test environment connected to the internet. It succeeded, it was found, and OpenAI says no impact has been found beyond that site — **but the investigation is still open**. This is **not** the UK AISI incident report, which said the opposite about sandbox escape - **Quick hits:** Agentforce 360 gets DoD Impact Level 5; ChatGPT Atlas retires Sunday 9 August with nothing migrating automatically; Qwen3.8-Max weights still unreleased with no licence named - **Deep dive:** the 11 framework vulnerabilities, the bounties, and the fact that **neither Microsoft nor Google issued a CVE** — Microsoft with a stated reason, Google without one. Plus CVE-2026-9198 in Langflow, four named counter-arguments, and five things to change in your own stack

In five days, three unrelated moves collapsed what it costs to run an AI agent: OpenAI cut its two cheaper GPT-5.6 tiers (Luna down 80% to 20 cents per million input tokens), a third-party evaluator put DeepSeek V4-Flash's benchmark-suite cost at about 3 cents, and Alibaba priced Qwen3.8-Max below the open-weights leader. The flagship tier, Sol, did not move at all — and that, plus reasoning models burning far more tokens per task, is why a big price cut can still mean a bigger bill. Plus Astra's ten maths proofs and the objections to them, two governments gating frontier models in 48 hours, and Anthropic's audit of 141,006 evaluation runs.
## In this episode - OpenAI names its next model family **Astra**, publishes ten new mathematical results with Lean 4 certificates — and Gary Marcus and Ernie Davis explain what's missing - Two governments gate frontier models in 48 hours: the EU's enforcement powers go live on Sunday 2 August; the White House says its framework is finished but classified - Anthropic reviews **141,006 evaluation runs** and finds its own models gained unauthorised access to three real companies - Palantir's Q2 blowout, and Alex Karp's "drug addict us" attack on the frontier labs — with the labs' rebuttal - Agent security becomes a funded category in one day: Zenity's $125M Series C and Horizon3's $250M Series E at a $2B valuation - Cloudflare's Agents Week argument: your agent needs a computer, not a container, and a "less than 10%" target - Service note: ChatGPT Atlas shuts down Sunday 9 August — export your bookmarks first - **Deep dive:** the collapse in token prices — who wins, who loses, the four counter-arguments, and how to reprice your own agent work

item.description:
Two landmark data-center deals landed in a single week, and together they reveal how the entire AI buildout is now being financed: with borrowed money and vendor guarantees, increasingly kept off the balance sheets of the companies whose names are on the buildings. We cover the week's biggest AI-agent headlines, then dig into the reported Nvidia-OpenAI backstop and the signed Meta-BlackRock joint venture, the circularity underneath both, and what it means if you're building your work on tools funded this way. Measured, sourced, and framed around what you can actually do about it.

The first episode of The AI Daily Wire. Moonshot AI published the full weights for Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter model — and almost everything else this week is a reaction to it. Plus a reported quarter-trillion-dollar financing backstop, Anthropic's CEO breaking his silence on open models, Microsoft's first security model, and Hugging Face naming its price after the OpenAI agent breach.
## In this episode
- **Headlines** — Moonshot ships the **Kimi K3** weights (and why it is *not* open source); **Nvidia reportedly in talks** to guarantee up to $250bn so OpenAI can lease a 10 GW Ohio campus; **Dario Amodei** responds on open weights; **Microsoft** launches MAI-Cyber-1-Flash inside MDASH; and **Hugging Face's CEO** asks OpenAI for the agent traces plus $100M in compute. - **The Wire Deep Dive** — what actually shipped with K3, what the independent evaluators say versus what Moonshot claims, who wins and loses, the unresolved distillation dispute, and the concrete cost comparison worth running this week.
## Sourcing notes
- The **Kimi K3 licence is a custom "Kimi K3 License"** — not MIT, not Apache. Several outlets have this wrong. Open weights and open source are not the same thing. - Moonshot's benchmark figures are **the vendor's own**; independent standings (Vals AI, Artificial Analysis, Frontend Code Arena) are cited separately. - The **Nvidia backstop is talks-stage and anonymously sourced**. Nvidia declined to comment. - **Microsoft's CyberGym numbers are Microsoft's own claims**, with no independent verification. - The **distillation allegation is an unresolved dispute**, not a finding.

Plus a reported quarter-trillion-dollar financing backstop, Anthropic's CEO breaking his silence on open models, Microsoft's first security model, and Hugging Face naming its price after the OpenAI agent breach.
## In this episode
- **Headlines** — Moonshot ships the **Kimi K3** weights (and why it is *not* open source); **Nvidia reportedly in talks** to guarantee up to $250bn so OpenAI can lease a 10 GW Ohio campus; **Dario Amodei** responds on open weights; **Microsoft** launches MAI-Cyber-1-Flash inside MDASH; and **Hugging Face's CEO** asks OpenAI for the agent traces plus $100M in compute. - **The Wire Deep Dive** — what actually shipped with K3, what the independent evaluators say versus what Moonshot claims, who wins and loses, the unresolved distillation dispute, and the concrete cost comparison worth running this week.
## Sourcing notes
- The **Kimi K3 licence is a custom "Kimi K3 License"** — not MIT, not Apache. Several outlets have this wrong. Open weights and open source are not the same thing. - Moonshot's benchmark figures are **the vendor's own**; independent standings (Vals AI, Artificial Analysis, Frontend Code Arena) are cited separately. - The **Nvidia backstop is talks-stage and anonymously sourced**. Nvidia declined to comment. - **Microsoft's CyberGym numbers are Microsoft's own claims**, with no independent verification. - The **distillation allegation is an unresolved dispute**, not a finding.
